title: Public vs Private Medical Colleges: What MDCAT Score Gets You Where
excerpt: Public and private medical colleges in Pakistan sit at very different points on the aggregate scale — and the fee gap between them is large enough to change how you think about your target score.

content.text: Two very different paths to the same degree

MBBS and BDS from a public medical college and MBBS and BDS from a private one lead to the same qualification, but the road to get there looks quite different — both in terms of the aggregate you'll need and what you'll pay along the way. Understanding that gap early can help you set a realistic target instead of aiming vaguely at "a good MDCAT score."

Every figure in this post — aggregates, fees, seat numbers — changes from year to year and college to college. Treat everything here as a general orientation to how public and private options compare, not as this year's exact numbers. Always check the current merit lists and fee notifications from the specific colleges and admitting bodies (UHS, KMU, or your provincial authority) you're targeting.
The aggregate gap is real and significant

Public medical colleges, particularly the well-known ones, tend to close admissions at aggregates that sit well into the high 80s and low-to-mid 90s percent range in recent cycles — and that's often just for open merit at top-tier institutions. Mid-tier public colleges and provincial-quota seats tend to close somewhat lower, though still solidly competitive.

Private medical colleges, by contrast, generally accept students across a much wider aggregate range, with many private seats going to students well below what a public college would require — sometimes into the mid-70s or lower, depending on the institution and the specific year.

This means the same MDCAT performance that wouldn't come close to a public open-merit seat could very realistically secure you a private one. Neither path is inherently "worse" — but it's worth understanding which door your realistic aggregate is likely to open before you commit your prep strategy to one specific target.
The fee difference is the part students underestimate

If the aggregate gap is significant, the fee gap is dramatic. Public medical colleges in Pakistan are heavily subsidized, with annual tuition typically in the tens of thousands of rupees — a small fraction of what a private seat costs for the same degree. Private medical college fees, by contrast, typically run into the millions of rupees per year, with some institutions charging considerably more than others depending on their fee structure and any regulatory caps in place.

Private MBBS fees in Pakistan are subject to a regulatory cap, though some institutions are exempt from it and charge above that cap. Fee structures and caps can change, so confirm the current figure directly with any private college you're seriously considering — this is not a number to estimate from an old blog post, including this one.

Put simply: a stronger MDCAT score doesn't just change which college accepts you. For many families, it directly determines whether medical school is financially a modest expense or a major, multi-year financial commitment. That's a meaningful reason to treat every additional MDCAT mark as valuable, not just as a number on a merit list.
It's not only about the price tag
Cost is the most visible difference, but it's not the only one worth weighing:

items: Public colleges are typically older, government-affiliated institutions, often with large teaching hospitals attached and a long track record
Private colleges vary more in age, infrastructure, and reputation — some are well-established with strong hospital affiliations, while newer ones are still building that track record
Seat availability differs too: public colleges generally offer far fewer total seats relative to the number of applicants, which is part of why their aggregates run so high

Admission processes can differ in structure — some provinces run centralized admission systems covering all affiliated public colleges, which is worth understanding for your specific province rather than assuming the same process applies everywhere

content.text: None of this means private is automatically a worse choice or public automatically the "right" one — it depends on your finances, your aggregate, and what matters to you in a medical education, including things a ranking or fee table won't capture, like a specific hospital affiliation or location close to home.
Rather than aiming for an abstract "high score," it's more useful to work backward from where you actually want to end up:

items: Calculate your current aggregate estimate using your Matric and FSc marks alongside a target MDCAT score

Compare that estimate against recent closing merits for the specific public colleges you're interested in — not just the most famous ones, since mid-tier public options may be more realistically in reach
If a private seat is a real possibility for your family, look into current fee structures early, since costs vary meaningfully between private institutions
Keep your target flexible until closer to results — closing merits shift year to year based on that year's applicant pool, so treat any single number as a reference point, not a guarantee

content.text: Our merit calculator can help you run these numbers with your own marks, and our Universities pages have more detail on specific public and private institutions if you want to compare options directly.

Public and private medical colleges in Pakistan sit at meaningfully different points on both the aggregate scale and the fee scale — and both gaps are large enough to shape a real decision, not just a preference. Understanding roughly where your realistic aggregate lands, and being honest early about what a private seat would cost if that's the direction you're likely headed, makes for a much more grounded MDCAT prep strategy than aiming at a single score in isolation. Always confirm the current year's actual figures — merits and fees both shift — before treating any specific number as your target.

items.question: What aggregate do I need for a public medical college in Pakistan?
items.answer: Top-tier public colleges tend to close open merit in the high 80s to low-mid 90s percent range in recent cycles. Mid-tier public colleges and provincial-quota seats tend to close somewhat lower, but still competitively — always check current merit lists rather than relying on past years.

items.question: Do private medical colleges accept lower MDCAT aggregates than public ones?
items.answer: Generally yes — private colleges accept students across a much wider aggregate range, with many seats going to students well below what a public college would require. The exact range depends on the specific institution and year.

items.question: How much more expensive is a private medical college compared to public?
items.answer: Substantially more. Public colleges are heavily subsidized, with annual tuition typically in the tens of thousands of rupees, while private college fees typically run into the millions per year — confirm current figures directly with any college you're considering.

items.question: Is a private medical college a worse choice than a public one?
items.answer: Not automatically — it depends on your finances, your aggregate, and factors a fee table doesn't capture, like hospital affiliation or location. Public colleges tend to have longer track records; private colleges vary more in age and reputation.

items.question: How should I set a realistic MDCAT target given these differences?
items.answer: Calculate your aggregate estimate from your Matric, FSc, and a target MDCAT score, then compare it against recent closing merits for specific colleges you're interested in — including mid-tier public options, not just the most famous ones — and research private fee structures early if that's a realistic path for your family.
